prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I would have come. When you called. But. I had the most beautiful pale pink rose. Its healthy stem was clenched between my teeth. And. Its thorns bit sharply into my tender wet flesh. So. I couldn't answer you. Still. My lips moved at you silently. They offered words you never heard. They screamed inside my crazed brain. Only. It could do nothing for you. In time the petals wilted. They blew away. And. They became compost in someone else's garden. The tough, fibrous stem withered. I bit down hard to snap its grip on me. Then. My teeth fell out. Its thorns had burrowed into my cheeks. They had implanted themselves permanently. They were suckling on my softest tissues. And. Not long after they sprouted tiny shoots. They coiled their way down. I still held the memory of your call. And. The long stemmed beauty lodged next to it. They cleaved unto the long roots curling down my neck. My body held tight and listened. Hard.

I would have answered your call. But something stopped me. A gorgeous rose, pale as blush, rested between my clenched teeth, its stem held firm. The thorns pierced deep into my soft, moist skin. Because of this, I stayed silent. Yet my mouth kept forming words meant for you—words you'd never hear, words trapped and shrieking within my fevered mind. None of it reached you, though.

As time passed, the petals dried up and scattered on the wind, eventually decomposing in a stranger's flowerbed. The stem, once tough and stringy, began to wilt. I clamped down forcefully to break free from its hold, and my teeth came loose in the process. The thorns had already burrowed into my cheeks, rooting themselves there for good, feeding on my most delicate flesh.

Soon after, tiny shoots emerged from where the thorns had settled, spiraling downward through my body. Your call remained a fixed memory within me, resting alongside that beautiful, long-stemmed intruder. Together they fastened onto the roots winding their way down my throat. My whole body went rigid, straining to listen.
outputs.L3:
I would have answered the call. I wanted to—desperately, urgently—but a pale pink rose was held fast between my teeth, its stem clenched so tightly that no sound could escape past it. The bloom pressed against my lips like a gag fashioned from something that should have been beautiful, its petals soft against my skin even as the rest of it betrayed me utterly.

The thorns were the cruelest part. They dug into the soft flesh of my mouth, tiny punctures that bloomed with pinpricks of blood each time I tried to speak. My lips moved anyway—shaping words, forming sentences, screaming silently into a void that swallowed every sound before it could take shape. The words piled up inside my skull, a pressure building behind my eyes, behind my teeth, behind everything, and still nothing emerged but the faintest whisper of air escaping around the stem.

Time did what time does. The petals, once so delicately pink, began to brown at their edges, curling inward like hands closing into fists. One by one they loosened their grip and drifted away, carried off by some wind I couldn't feel, scattering into memory. The stem, no longer sustained by whatever strange life had animated it, grew brittle and gray. I bit down, desperate now, feeling my own teeth crack and splinter against the woody fiber, trying to break free of this thing that had claimed my voice. Tooth after tooth gave way, falling from my gums like small white stones, and still the stem held its ground, unyielding even as it died.

But dying, it turned out, was not the same as leaving. The thorns that had wounded me found purchase in that wounding—they burrowed deeper, past skin and muscle, anchoring themselves permanently into the soft tissue of my cheeks. From those buried points, something new began to grow. Shoots pushed outward through my flesh, pale green and impossibly persistent, while roots spread downward and inward, threading themselves through nerve and sinew. They wove themselves into the very fabric of my body, and somehow—inexplicably—into the fabric of that unanswered call, as though the memory of it had become as physical as bone.

I am changed now, permanently and completely. My body no longer belongs entirely to me; it belongs also to the rose that consumed my voice, to the roots that have made a home of my throat and jaw. I hold still, because stillness is what the roots seem to require, and I listen—achingly, intently—as I feel them curl slowly down the column of my neck, spreading further with each passing moment, claiming more of me in their quiet, relentless growth. The call I never answered echoes somewhere inside that silence, and I wonder if it will ever stop ringing, or if I have simply become another kind of listener, rooted in place, waiting for an answer I can no longer give.

# The Rose I Could Not Put Down

The phone rang, and I could not answer it.

I want you to understand this literally, not as some metaphor I am dressing up in prettier clothes. There was a rose—pink, the color of the inside of a shell, the color of something that should never be exposed to air—and its stem was between my teeth. I do not remember picking it up. I do not remember choosing to hold it there. I only remember the ringing, insistent and far away, and the way my jaw had already locked around the thorns as though some older, wiser part of me had decided this was necessary.

The thorns bit into the soft flesh of my inner cheeks. I could taste copper mixing with the strange green sweetness of the stem. And the phone kept ringing.

I tried to speak. I want that understood too—I tried. My tongue pressed against the stem, my lips moved around it, shaping words that had nowhere to go. Hello. Wait. I'm here. Don't hang up. All of it collapsed into silence before it could become sound, swallowed by the thing I could not release. The rose sat heavy and fragrant against my tongue, petals brushing the roof of my mouth like something trying to whisper directly into my skull, bypassing my throat entirely, bypassing the part of me that might have found words.

Whoever was calling did not know about the rose. How could they? From the outside, I imagine I looked merely still. Perhaps distracted. Perhaps rude, for not picking up, for letting it ring and ring until it stopped, and then ring again later, and stop again. They could not see the thorns anchoring me in place, could not taste the strange perfume flooding the back of my throat, could not know that I was screaming inside a silence I had not chosen and could not break.

Days passed this way. Or maybe it was longer. Time behaves strangely when you are holding something instead of saying something.

The petals began to droop first—that impossible shell-pink darkening to the color of a bruise, then to brown, then to something with no color at all, just texture, just papery fragility crumbling against my lips. I thought, foolishly, that this meant release. I thought a wilted thing surely loses its grip.

I was wrong.

As the flower died, the thorns did not loosen. They did the opposite. They pressed deeper, as though the dying plant understood something about permanence that I did not yet grasp—as though it knew that to lose its bloom, it needed to root itself more thoroughly in whatever it had been given. And what it had been given was me: my mouth, my jaw, the tender places thorns are not meant to go.

I felt them push past the simple bloodied punctures and into something more essential. Not just skin now. Not just flesh. I felt them find the nerve, the marrow, the deep quiet architecture where memory lives. And there, impossibly, unbearably, they began to grow.

Not the flower—the flower was long gone, reduced to dust and desiccated fragments that I sometimes still find on my tongue when I wake. But the roots. The roots had never needed the bloom to justify their expansion. They spread through me the way roots do underground, blind and patient and unstoppable, seeking the softest, wettest places to anchor themselves.

They found the call.

I do not know how else to explain this except to say that the roots grew directly into my memory of the ringing phone, of the number I never saw, of the voice I never heard and now never will. The unanswered call became trellis and soil at once—something for the roots to climb, something for them to feed on. Every time I try to remember what I could have said, what I might have heard, I feel the tug of thorns instead, deep in whatever part of me holds such things.

This is why I still do not speak of it easily. Not because the rose is still in my mouth—it isn't, not physically, not anymore. My jaw has long since unclenched. My lips can form words freely now, can shape hellos and goodbyes and every ordinary thing a mouth is meant to do.

But underneath, where no one else can see, the roots remain. They have wound themselves so completely around that missed call, that voice I'll never identify, that message I'll never receive, that I cannot access the memory without also touching the thorns. I cannot think of that ringing phone without tasting blood and rose-dust, without feeling that old useless pressure of trying to speak around something lodged too deep to move.

So when people ask why I go quiet sometimes, why certain silences seem to swallow me whole, I do not tell them about the rose. How could I? It sounds absurd, spoken aloud—thorns and roots and a phone call decades old, tangled together like some grotesque garden growing in the dark beneath my ribs.

Instead, I simply say I am remembering something. This is true, in its way. I am always remembering something, and it is always rooted, and it always tastes faintly of copper and pink, sweet and cutting all at once—the flavor of everything I once could not say, and still, in the end, cannot.
outputs.L5:
# On Moments That Matter

When we look back on our lives, certain moments stand out with startling clarity—a decision made, a conversation overheard, a single afternoon that changed everything. We often don't recognize these turning points as they happen. Only later, with the benefit of hindsight, do we understand their true weight.

But recognizing significance after the fact is a strange kind of wisdom. It comes too late to change our choices, yet early enough to shape how we tell our story. We build narratives around these pivotal moments, weaving cause and effect into something that feels meaningful, even inevitable.

Its power lies precisely in this retrospective clarity. The past, unlike the present, holds still long enough for us to study it. We can trace the threads of consequence, understand how one small choice led to another, and see the shape of a life as it actually unfolded—not as we feared or hoped it might.

When someone asks us what moment changed everything, we rarely hesitate. The answer surfaces almost instantly, as if it had been waiting patiently for the question. But the truth is messier than any single story can capture. Change rarely arrives in one dramatic instant. More often, it accumulates quietly—in a thousand small moments we never thought to count.

Its lesson, perhaps, is this: we are always living inside our own turning points, even when we cannot see them. The present moment, however ordinary it feels, may someday become the story we tell about how everything changed.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal short prose poem about failing to answer someone's call because of an obsession, using a rose as the central metaphor.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Rose Answers Instead

The phone rings and I am counting petals again. Seventeen. No—eighteen, if you count the one curling inward like a fist that changed its mind about hitting something.

Your name lights the screen in a color I've started calling *missing*. The rose does not care. The rose has never cared about anything except the slow architecture of its own unfolding, each petal a small decision made and unmade in the same breath.

I tell myself: one more ring. One more layer. Somewhere beneath the fifth or sixth spiral there must be a center, a place where the flower stops becoming and simply *is*—but roses are liars shaped like promises, and I am a fool shaped like someone who used to answer phones.

The ringing stops. The silence after has thorns.

I go back to counting. Twenty-three. Twenty-four. The numbers mean nothing—they never meant anything—but my hands have forgotten how to do anything else, and my hands are the only part of me still speaking to you, in this language of missed calls and interrupted flowers.

Somewhere you are pressing the phone to your ear, listening to it not-ring, and I am here, listening to petals fall like every word I should have said, arranging themselves into a shape that almost—almost—looks like *sorry*.

The rose does not apologize. The rose simply continues, red and relentless, blooming its way toward winter while I count and count and count, my fingers stained with a color that might be love or might just be the absence of you, pressed flat between the pages of whatever book I'll pretend I was always reading.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of experimental flash fiction with short, fragmented sentences (using "So." and "Then." as standalone lines) about guilt and silence.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Water Kept**

The lake took him in nine seconds.

So.

I counted. Standing there. Counting instead of screaming.

Nine seconds and the surface closed like a mouth that had said enough already.

Then.

Nothing.

The water went back to being water. Flat. Indifferent. Sunlight doing its usual work on the ripples until even those forgot to exist.

I did not move.

So.

This is the part where I should say I dove in. Where I should say my body knew before my mind did, some animal instinct overriding the cold arithmetic of fear. But no.

I stood on the dock.

I counted.

Then.

They found him an hour later. Face the color of the moon we couldn't see yet because it was only four in the afternoon. Face like a question nobody wanted to ask.

His mother made a sound I still hear.

I did not make any sound at all.

So.

Here is the silence: I told them I was too far away. I told them the current took him before I understood what was happening. I told them a version soft enough to live inside.

The truth stayed underwater with him.

Then.

Years accumulate like sediment. You'd think guilt erodes. It doesn't. It just gets buried under other years, other silences, smaller ones that practice on you until you're fluent.

I go to the lake sometimes.

I stand on the dock.

So.

The water still doesn't say anything. It never did. That was always me, projecting confession onto something that only reflects.

Nine seconds. I've done the math a thousand times. Nine seconds of standing there, doing nothing, would not have been enough time to save him even if I'd moved.

This does not help.

Then.

Some nights I open my mouth at dinner, at the grocery store, in the middle of ordinary conversations, and I feel the whole story rising like something displaced, like water finding its level—

And I close it again.

So.

The dock still stands. Gray wood, warping slowly into the shape of forgetting.

I stand there some afternoons and I do not count anything.

I let the seconds pass uncounted, the way they should have the first time, the way silence maybe deserves: unmeasured, unproven, unforgiven.

Then.

Nothing.

The lake keeps its nine seconds.

I keep mine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic monologue in a strange, disjointed style about a person choking on a rose stem while someone they love tries to reach them.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Rose Does Not Apologize**

There is a stem in my throat and it is
blooming—no, wrong word, blooms are for
gardens, for Sundays, for hands that don't
shake like this—

petals opening backward down my esophagus
red unfurling into red into a red I cannot
cough into language
you are saying my name like it's
a rope but ropes don't taste like
copper, like green sap, like
the inside of a stem that keeps
growing even now, even here,
even as your hand—

*I see your hand*

—reaches, reaches, the way water reaches
for a drain, helpless-shaped, and I think
*this is what drowning looks like from inside
a garden* and I think *thorns don't ask permission*
and I think of nothing, actually, thinking
is the first thing to go, before breath,
before your face which is doing something
complicated and terrified and beautiful in the
worst possible way—

You are three feet away.
You are three hundred years away.
The distance between a body and the body
that would save it is measured in
something other than feet, in something
like the space between a flower's name
and the fact of it, between *rose*
and *this thing lodged in me, unrose-ing me*

I want to tell you it doesn't hurt
the way you think it does—
it hurts like being *full* of spring
when spring was never invited in,
it hurts like green things insisting
on their green-ness in a place
built for red only, for singular red,
for the red of trying to speak
and getting flowers instead of words—

Your hand is closer now.
Your hand is a decade away.

I am becoming a vase.
I am becoming the thing that holds
instead of the thing that speaks.

Reach faster.
Reach faster.

The stem is patient.
The stem has all the time
that I am running out of—

and you, love, you
are still reaching,
still three feet, still three hundred years,
still the only greenhouse
I would ever choose
to die inside of.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dark, body-horror style prose poem exploring themes of regret and transformation, where a flower's thorns grow into the speaker's flesh.
counterfactuals.output:
# What Blooms Beneath

I planted regret in the soft meat behind my sternum, and it grew.

At first, only a stem—thin, green, unremarkable. I told myself I could pull it out anytime. I told myself many things.

The thorns came second.

They pierced outward from the inside, small hooked mouths breaking through skin that had never asked to become soil. Each one a sentence I didn't say, a door I didn't close, a name I let dissolve on my tongue rather than speak into the room where it might have mattered. I felt them stitch themselves into muscle, into the white lattice of rib, patient as guilt always is.

I did not scream. Screaming would have required breath I no longer fully owned.

By the second week, the petals unfurled through the gaps between my fingers—obscene, velvet, the color of old wounds trying to look like sunsets. People said *how lovely*. They did not see the roots wrapping the ladder of my spine, drinking what marrow remained, translating years into chlorophyll.

I understand now: this is what regret does when you let it stay too long. It does not remain a feeling. It becomes architecture. It becomes the thing your body is *for*.

Some mornings I find new thorns pushing through the meat of my palm—each one shaped like a word I swallowed instead of speaking, each one blooming into the shape of a face I turned away from. The flower does not ask permission. It never did. It simply took the silence I offered and built a garden from it, rib by rib, until I could not tell where the grief ended and the green began.

I am mostly stem now. Mostly root.

Somewhere beneath the flowering wreck of what I was, something that used to be a person keeps whispering: *you could have just said sorry. You could have just said it once.*

But the flower has my throat.

The flower has had it for years.

And still—still—it blooms so beautifully that strangers stop to admire what regret can make of a body that refused, again and again, to speak.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract, emotionally intense piece of literary fiction using very short sentences and repeated words like "And." and "Only." to convey a character's internal breakdown after missing an important call.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Missed Call

The phone rang. She saw it ring. She did not answer.

And then it stopped.

Only silence.

She stared at the screen. Three missed calls. Dad. Dad. Dad. The last one, forty-three seconds long. Long enough to leave a message. She did not check it yet.

And her hands were still.

Only they were not still. They were shaking, and she watched them shake like they belonged to someone else. Some other woman standing in some other kitchen holding some other phone.

She had been busy. That was all. Just busy. Folding towels. The dryer had buzzed. She had been folding towels and the phone had rung on the counter and she had thought: later. I'll call him later.

And later came.

Only later did not look like she thought it would.

She pressed the voicemail. Her thumb moved without her. Some animal instinct now, some machinery beneath thought. The message began.

His voice. Small. Smaller than she remembered. Saying her name. Saying it's nothing, sweetheart, just wanted to hear your voice. Saying call me back when you can. No rush.

No rush.

And the towels were folded now. All of them. Stacked white and clean on the counter like nothing had happened. Like the world had not tilted on some invisible axis while she matched socks and smoothed wrinkles from a dish towel.

She called back.

It rang once.

And twice.

Only it kept ringing. Four times. Five. Voicemail.

She called again.

Ring. Ring. Ring.

And nothing.

She sat down on the kitchen floor. The tile was cold through her jeans. She noticed this the way she noticed everything now — sideways, distant, like weather happening to another country.

Her phone in her lap. Her hands not her hands. Her heart doing something enormous and terrible in her chest, some slow drum building toward a sound she did not want to hear.

She thought: he is fine. He is in the garden. He does not always hear the phone.

And she thought: he called three times.

Only three times was not nothing. Three times was a man trying.

She dialed her sister. It rang once and her sister picked up already crying and that was how she knew. That was the whole answer, right there, in the half-second before words. Crying meant already. Crying meant too late. Crying meant the towels had still been folding themselves into perfect squares while the actual world ended forty miles away.

She did not remember standing up. She did not remember the keys, or the door, or backing out of the driveway. She remembered only the number 43. Forty-three seconds. That was how long she had to have picked up the phone. That was how long it would have taken to say hello, and to hear whatever he needed to say, and to say it back to him before it was too late to say anything at all.

Forty-three seconds. She could have given him forty-three seconds.

And she had given him towels instead.

Only there was no such thing as later, not really. Later was a lie the mind told itself to keep from feeling the shape of now. And now the phone sat silent in the cupholder, screen dark, already a relic of some earlier version of the day — the one where he was still reachable, still just a ring away, still someone she could call back.

She drove. The road blurred at the edges. Her whole body a fist around some center that would not hold.

And somewhere behind her the towels sat clean and folded and white.

Only nothing was clean now. Nothing was folded into its place. The dryer had stopped its buzzing hours ago but something kept ringing, kept ringing, kept ringing in her, a phone that would never be answered again, a voice already gone into the machine of the past, saying no rush, sweetheart, saying take your time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
